modules.title: Squid Proxy
modules.sum: Run your first caching forward proxy: install Squid, open it to your LAN, filter sites with ACLs and speed up repeat visits with caching.

lessons.title: What is Squid Proxy (and why it is first)
lessons.sum: Forward vs reverse proxies, what caching buys you, and where Squid sits between your LAN and the internet.

blocks.x: Your first topic is **Squid Proxy** because it touches everything else you will learn: networking, services, files and security — in one small, visible project. A client asks Squid, Squid asks the internet, then Squid answers the client — and remembers the answer for next time.
Forward proxy vs reverse proxy

x: **Forward proxy (Squid default)** — sits near the clients. Your laptop and classmates point their browsers at Squid, and Squid fetches the web for them. Good for caching, filtering and saving bandwidth.
**Reverse proxy (nginx)** — sits in front of a server. The internet talks to nginx, nginx talks to your app. Good for TLS and serving sites.
This module is about the **forward** side: one Squid box serving a whole classroom or office LAN.

blocks.x: What caching buys you

blocks.title: The idea in one picture
blocks.x:
# without proxy: every client fetches from the internet
# laptop -> internet   (100 MB downloaded 30x = 3000 MB)
#
# with Squid: first client fills the cache, the rest reuse it
# laptop  -> squid (3128) -> internet
# laptop2 -> squid (HIT from cache, no download)
#
# point a client at Squid for a quick test:
export http_proxy=http://192.168.1.10:3128
export https_proxy=http://192.168.1.10:3128
curl -I http://example.com
Think of Squid as a shared notebook: the first student looks up the answer online and writes it down; the next 29 students just read the notebook. Same web, far less waiting.
A forward proxy sees the domains you visit. Only point your devices at a Squid you or your school runs — never a random proxy IP from the internet.

quiz.q: Where does a forward proxy like Squid sit?
opts: In front of a web server, facing the internet
Near the clients — clients ask Squid, Squid asks the internet
quiz.why: A forward proxy serves clients on your LAN; a reverse proxy sits in front of servers. Squid defaults to the forward side.

quiz.q: What is the main win of Squid caching on a classroom LAN?
opts: It makes the internet faster for everyone else
Repeat downloads are served from Squid instead of re-downloading
It removes the need for IP addresses
quiz.why: The first fetch fills the cache; later identical requests are HITs served locally — less bandwidth, faster loads.

lessons.title: Install and run Squid
lessons.sum: Install Squid on Ubuntu, open port 3128, point a client at it and prove caching works.

blocks.x: Squid is one package, one config file and one port: **3128**. Install it, start it, then tell one client to use it before you open it to the whole LAN.
Install and check

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y squid
sudo systemctl enable --now squid
sudo systemctl status squid --no-pager
ss -tlnp | grep 3128
The two lines that matter in squid.conf

blocks.title: /etc/squid/squid.conf (essentials)
blocks.x:
http_port 3128
acl localnet src 192.168.0.0/16
http_access allow localnet
Prove it from a client

export http_proxy=http://192.168.1.10:3128 https_proxy=http://192.168.1.10:3128
curl -I http://example.com
`squid -k parse` before every reload, and `journalctl -u squid -n 50` when it misbehaves.
Default Squid only allows localhost. Until you add your LAN to `localnet`, other devices get access-denied — that is the safe default, not a bug.

quiz.q: Which port does Squid listen on by default?
quiz.why: 3128 is the classic Squid forward-proxy port.

quiz.q: Safe order after editing squid.conf?
opts: Run `squid -k parse` to validate, then reload
quiz.why: Validate first with `squid -k parse`, then reload.

lessons.title: ACLs, filtering and caching
lessons.sum: Allow your LAN, block time-wasting sites, set cache size and read the logs.

blocks.x: Once Squid runs, the real work is **who may use it and what they may fetch**. That is all done with ACLs plus a few cache knobs.
Allow the classroom, block the distractions

blocks.title: /etc/squid/squid.conf — access rules
blocks.x:
acl lan src 192.168.1.0/24
acl blocked dstdomain .games.example .video.example
http_access deny blocked
http_access allow lan
http_access deny all

x: Order matters: a `deny blocked` line must sit **above** the broad `allow lan`, or it never triggers.
Start with one LAN range — opening to `all` turns your box into an open relay for strangers.

blocks.x: Cache size and logs

cache_dir ufs /var/spool/squid 2000 16 256
maximum_object_size 128 MB
# watch the log: first visit TCP_MISS, refresh TCP_HIT:
# sudo tail -f /var/log/squid/access.log
Refresh the same page twice while tailing access.log — MISS then HIT is the moment Squid clicks.
HTTPS bodies are encrypted, so Squid caches the connection setup but not the page content unless you do full TLS interception.

quiz.q: Why must `deny blocked` come before `allow lan`?
opts: Squid uses the first matching rule, so the specific deny has to win first
quiz.why: Squid stops at the first match. A broad allow placed first would swallow the deny.

quiz.q: In access.log, what does TCP_HIT mean?
opts: Squid served it from cache without re-downloading
quiz.why: TCP_MISS is fetched from the internet; TCP_HIT is served from the local cache.

modules.title: Linux Essentials
modules.sum: Understand what Linux actually is, log in for the first time, and learn your way around the filesystem of a fresh server.

lessons.title: What is Linux (and why servers love it)
lessons.sum: Kernel vs distribution, the big distro families, and how to pick a server operating system you can live with.

blocks.x: A **Linux server** is just a computer you reach over the network: no monitor, no mouse, and instead of a desktop you get a shell. This course is about being fluent in that environment.
Kernel vs distribution

Strictly speaking, Linux is only the **kernel** — the piece that talks to hardware, schedules processes and manages memory. What you actually install is a **distribution**: the kernel plus a package manager, shells, libraries and tools, packaged and maintained together.

x: **Debian family** — Debian, Ubuntu, Mint. Package manager: `apt`. The most common choice for beginners and web servers.
**Red Hat family** — RHEL, Fedora, AlmaLinux, Rocky. Package manager: `dnf`. Common in enterprises.
**SUSE family** — openSUSE, SUSE Linux Enterprise. Package manager: `zypper`.
**Others** — Alpine (tiny; huge in containers), Arch (rolling release, build-it-yourself).

blocks.x: Why the internet runs on Linux servers

x: Free and open source — you can inspect it, script it and ship it.
Stable: years of uptime is normal, not newsworthy.
Remote-first: SSH and a shell are enough to run everything.
Automation-friendly: every task is a command you can repeat and schedule.
Scales from a Raspberry Pi to server farms with thousands of machines.

blocks.x: Which distro should you learn on?

Pick one and stay with it for a while. For a first server, an **Ubuntu LTS** or **Debian stable** machine is the safest choice — enormous community, tutorials everywhere. Everything you learn transfers to the other distros.

blocks.title: See what you're running
blocks.x:
cat /etc/os-release   # distribution name and version
uname -r              # kernel version
This course uses Debian/Ubuntu commands (`apt`, `ufw`, `/var/log/syslog`). When something differs on the Red Hat family, a note will tell you — e.g. `dnf` instead of `apt`.
Don't judge Linux by a desktop you tried once. Server Linux is a much calmer world: text files, services and logs — and nobody will ever ask you to install printer drivers.

quiz.q: What does a distribution add on top of the Linux kernel?
opts: A package manager, shells, libraries and user-space tools
Nothing — the words mean the same thing
quiz.why: The kernel drives the hardware; the distribution is everything around it: package manager, core utilities, init system, documentation and default services.

quiz.q: Which command prints the distribution name and version?
quiz.why: `/etc/os-release` describes the distribution. `uname -r` shows only the kernel version.

lessons.title: Your first login: reading the shell
lessons.sum: What the prompt is really telling you, how to size up a machine in ten seconds, and how to get help without leaving the terminal.

blocks.x: You will meet a server through a **shell** — nearly always `bash` — over an SSH connection. The first skill is not typing commands, it is understanding what the screen already tells you.

blocks.title: First contact
blocks.x:
ssh deploy@203.0.113.10

Welcome to Ubuntu LTS
Last login: Sun Oct  4 21:58:12 2026 from 198.51.100.7
deploy@web-01:~$
Anatomy of the prompt

x: `deploy` — the user you are logged in as.
`web-01` — the hostname. **Check it** before anything destructive; production looks exactly like staging.
`~` — your current directory; `~` is shorthand for your home directory.
`$` — a normal user. A `#` here means **root**, where every typo is a loaded weapon.

blocks.x: Sizing up the machine in ten seconds

whoami    # which user am I?
hostname  # which machine is this?
uptime    # uptime and load averages
uname -a  # kernel and architecture
cat /etc/os-release
Getting help without leaving the terminal

x: `man grep` — the manual page. `q` quits, `/` searches inside the page.
`grep --help` — quick summary of flags.
`man 5 crontab` — the number picks a manual section; section 5 is file formats.
`apropos 'copy files'` — search manuals by keyword when you forget a command name.

blocks.x: Live in the shell and it will love you back: **Tab** completes command and file names, the **up arrow** replays history, and `history | grep ssh` finds that command from last week.
Copy-pasting commands from the internet is how servers get compromised. Read every command before running it — especially anything containing `sudo`, `curl | sh` or `rm`.

quiz.q: The prompt ends with `#` instead of `$`. What does that mean?
opts: You are in a read-only directory
You are root — commands can modify anything
You are connected through a proxy
quiz.why: `#` is the traditional root prompt. Slow down and double-check paths when you see it.

quiz.q: Which key lists suggestions and completes names as you type?
quiz.why: Tab completion works for commands, paths and many arguments. Press it twice when unsure.

lessons.title: A tour of the filesystem
lessons.sum: What lives where: a map of /, absolute vs relative paths, and moving around a server without getting lost.

blocks.x: On a Linux server **everything is a file**, and there is a single tree that starts at `/`. Extra disks do not get drive letters — they get **mounted** into that tree.
The directories you will actually use

x: `/etc` — configuration. Nearly every service keeps its settings here.
`/var` — variable data: logs in `/var/log`, mail, caches, databases.
`/home` — one directory per human user.
`/root` — the root user's home directory (not `/home/root`).
`/usr` — installed programs, libraries and documentation.
`/opt` — add-on software installed as a bundle.
`/tmp` — scratch space, wiped on reboot. Never store anything you love here.
`/proc`, `/sys`, `/dev` — virtual files that expose the kernel, hardware and devices.

blocks.x: Moving around

pwd                 # where am I?
ls -lah /var/log    # all files, sizes, long format
cd /etc/nginx       # absolute path
cd ..               # up one level
cd -                # back to the previous directory
cd ~                # home
Absolute vs relative paths

A path starting with `/` is **absolute**: it means the same thing from anywhere. Anything else is **relative** to your current directory. Scripts should always use absolute paths, so they behave the same no matter who runs them.
`ls -lat /var/log` (newest first) is the fastest way to see what changed recently. `ls -lah` reveals hidden dotfiles and shows sizes in KB/MB instead of bytes.
Wildcards are expanded by the **shell** before the command even runs. `rm *.log` deletes whatever matches in *that* directory — run `ls *.log` first and look at the list before you delete it.

quiz.q: Where do most system and service logs live?
quiz.why: `/var` holds variable data, and `/var/log` is the traditional home of logs — one of the first places to look when something misbehaves.

quiz.q: Which of these is an absolute path?
quiz.why: Only a leading `/` anchors the path to the root of the tree. Everything else depends on where you currently are.

modules.title: Files & Text Power Tools
modules.sum: Create, read, search and delete files safely — then glue small commands together with pipes like a proper sysadmin.

lessons.title: Files and directories: the core moves
lessons.sum: Create, copy, move, read and (carefully) delete files, plus symlinks, file types and sizes.

blocks.x: Most server work is creating, reading, moving and deleting files. Own these few commands and everything else gets easier.
Create and organise

mkdir -p /srv/app/{logs,data}    # nested directories in one shot
touch /srv/app/.env               # create an empty file
cp -r /srv/app /srv/app-backup    # recursive copy
mv old-name.txt new-name.txt      # rename (instant, same filesystem)
mv notes.txt /tmp/                # move to another directory
Read without opening an editor

cat /etc/hostname            # print the whole file
less /etc/nginx/nginx.conf   # scroll; q quits, / searches
head -n 20 /var/log/syslog   # first 20 lines
tail -n 50 /var/log/syslog   # last 50 lines
tail -f /var/log/syslog      # follow live; Ctrl+C stops
Delete carefully

rm notes.txt
rm -r old-project/    # directory and everything in it
rm -i important.txt   # ask before each deletion

**There is no recycle bin.** `rm -rf` deletes recursively, without prompts, no matter how tired you are. Check the path with `pwd` and `ls` first, and dry-run destructive helpers (`find ... -print` before `-delete`).
Links, types and sizes

ln -s /opt/app/releases/2026-10-04 /opt/app/current  # symlink
ls -l            # first char:  - file, d directory, l symlink
file archive.bin # what is this really?
stat report.pdf  # size, owner, timestamps
du -sh /var/log  # disk used by a whole tree
Symlinks are how deployments flip versions with zero downtime: point `current` at the new release folder, then restart the service. A broken symlink shows up clearly in `ls -l`.

quiz.q: Which command creates `/srv/app/logs` even though `/srv/app` does not exist yet?
quiz.why: `-p` creates missing parent directories and stays quiet if the target already exists.

quiz.q: What does `rm -rf build/` do when `build/` is the wrong directory?
opts: It moves the directory to a trash folder
It deletes everything under it immediately and permanently
It fails unless you are root
quiz.why: -r recurses, -f never prompts. There is no undo — always verify the path before pressing Enter.

lessons.title: Find anything: files with find, text with grep
lessons.sum: Answer where is it? and where is it mentioned? for any file on the machine — and act on the results safely.

blocks.x: Two tools cover almost every search on a server: **find** for files, **grep** for the text inside them. Learn the four or five flags you will actually use.
find: locate files by almost anything

find /var/log -name '*.log' -size +10M     # logs bigger than 10 MB
find /srv -type f -name '*.conf'            # files only, by name
find /srv/app -type f -mtime -7             # changed in the last 7 days
find /tmp -type f -mtime +30 -print         # older than 30 days: preview first
find /srv/app -type f -exec chown app:app {} +  # run a command per hit

x: `-type f` files, `-type d` directories.
`-size +10M` bigger than 10 MB; `-size -1k` smaller than 1 KB; `+1G` gigabytes.
`-mtime -7` modified less than 7 days ago; `+7` more than 7 days ago.
`-iname` is the case-insensitive version of `-name`.

blocks.x: Always run the search first (the default `-print`) and eyeball the list **before** adding `-delete` or a destructive `-exec`. `find` is a chainsaw that hides its blade until you add an action.
grep: find text inside files

grep -rin 'timeout' /etc/nginx/   # recursive, ignore case, line numbers
grep -c 'ERROR' app.log           # count matching lines
grep -v '^#' nginx.conf           # hide comments (invert the match)
grep -E '50[0-9] ' access.log     # extended regex: 500 to 509
The killer combination

grep -rl 'old-domain.com' /etc              # which config files mention it?
find /srv -name '*.conf' -exec grep -l 'listen' {} +   # find, then filter by content
`grep -rl` (recursive, list file names only) is usually the fastest path to the answer — it stops you from dumping megabytes of log lines into the terminal.
`grep -r /` will happily crawl your whole disk and take minutes. Narrow the path to the directory you suspect — `/etc/nginx`, not `/`.

quiz.q: Which command finds log files larger than 10 MB in /var/log?
quiz.why: `find -size +10M` means strictly larger than 10 MB. Prefix `+` means greater than, `-` smaller than.

quiz.q: Search for 'timeout' anywhere under /etc, ignoring case, printing line numbers:
quiz.why: -r recurses, -i ignores case, -n prints line numbers. That trio covers most real-world greps.

lessons.title: Pipes and redirection: the superpower
lessons.sum: stdout, stderr, pipes and exit codes — the plumbing that turns small commands into one-liners that feel like magic.

blocks.x: The Unix philosophy in one sentence: **small tools that do one thing, connected by pipes**. Once you see I/O as plumbing, the command line becomes a Lego set.
Three streams: stdin, stdout, stderr

x: **stdin** (0) — input, usually your keyboard.
**stdout** (1) — normal output.
**stderr** (2) — errors. Keeping errors separate is what keeps logs readable.

blocks.x:
ls /var/log > listing.txt     # stdout to a file (overwrite)
ls /var/log >> listing.txt    # append instead of overwrite
mycmd 2> errors.log           # send stderr to its own file
mycmd > all.log 2>&1          # both streams into one file
mycmd > /dev/null 2>&1        # discard everything (handy in cron)
Pipes: stdout of one command becomes stdin of the next

blocks.title: The classic one-liner
blocks.x:
awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -5
# extract column 1 (IPs) → sort → count duplicates → rank → top 5

Read it as a pipeline: `awk` pulls the first column, `sort` groups equal values together, `uniq -c` counts each run, `sort -nr` ranks numerically, `head -5` keeps the winners. Five tiny tools, one answer: **your five noisiest visitors**.
Handy companions

x: `wc -l` — count lines.
`sort -h` — sort by human sizes (1K, 2M, 3G...).
`cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd` — print the first colon-separated field.
`tr 'A-Z' 'a-z'` — lowercase everything passing through.
`tee disk.txt` — write to a file **and** pass the data on: `df -h | tee disk.txt`.

blocks.x: Exit codes, && and ||
Every command exits with a number: `0` means success, anything else is a failure. `$?` holds the last one — and the shell operators read it for you.

apt update && apt upgrade -y       # upgrade only if update succeeded
systemctl is-active nginx || echo 'nginx is DOWN'
echo $?                             # exit code of the previous command
`grep -q pattern file` searches quietly: no output, only the exit code. Perfect for `&&` chains and scripts.
`>` opens (and truncates!) the target file **before** the command runs. `sort big.log > big.log` sorts an empty file. Use a new name or a temp file when input and output might be the same.

quiz.q: What is the difference between `>` and `>>`?
opts: `>` overwrites the file, `>>` appends to it
quiz.why: `>` truncates the target first — one wrong path and the old contents are gone. `>>` adds to the end.

quiz.q: In `mycmd > all.log 2>&1`, where does stderr end up?
quiz.why: `2>&1` points stream 2 (stderr) at stream 1 (stdout), which is already going to all.log — so both land in the file.

lessons.title: Survival editing and tar archives
lessons.sum: Edit config files with nano or vim without panicking, and bundle files for backup or transfer with tar.

blocks.x: Sooner or later you must edit a config file and bundle some files for transfer. This is the survival kit for both — no IDE required.
nano: the friendly editor

sudo nano /etc/nginx/sites-available/default
# Ctrl+O = save  ·  Ctrl+X = exit  ·  Ctrl+W = search
vim: worth ten minutes of your life

x: `i` enters insert mode (you can type). `Esc` returns to normal mode.
`:w` saves · `:q` quits · `:wq` saves and quits · `:q!` quits and throws changes away.
`/text` searches, `n` jumps to the next hit. `dd` deletes a line, `u` undoes.
Run `vimtutor` on any server — a guided half-hour that pays for itself forever.

blocks.x: Before editing a config by hand, copy it: `sudo cp nginx.conf nginx.conf.bak`. After editing, validate it: `sudo nginx -t` or `sudo sshd -t`. A syntax check beats an outage at 2 AM.
tar: bundle files the server way

tar -czvf backup.tar.gz /srv/app          # create · gzip · verbose · file
tar -tzf backup.tar.gz                     # list contents, no extraction
tar -xzvf backup.tar.gz -C /restore        # extract into a directory
tar -xzvf backup.tar.gz srv/app/index.html # extract a single file
zip -r site.zip site/                      # zip, when Windows users are involved

x: Letter mnemonic: `c` create, `x` extract, `t` list, `z` gzip, `v` talkative, `f` file. Order barely matters (`-zxvf` works fine).

blocks.x: `tar` writes paths relative to the extraction directory. Extracting a crafted archive as root in `/` can overwrite system files. Always extract with `-C` into a scratch directory first and look at what came out.

quiz.q: Which command extracts `backup.tar.gz` into `/restore`?
quiz.why: `-x` extracts, `-z` handles gzip, `-C` changes to the target directory before unpacking.

quiz.q: In vim, how do you quit **without** saving changes?
quiz.why: `:q!` forces a quit and discards modifications. `:wq` would save them, which is usually the opposite of what you want mid-edit.

modules.title: Users, Groups & Permissions
modules.sum: Know who exists on the machine, escalate to root the professional way, and give every file exactly the access it needs.

lessons.title: Users and groups: who is on this machine?
lessons.sum: Account types, the three files that define them, and how to create, inspect and remove users the right way.

blocks.x: Every process runs **as some user**. Server security starts with knowing who can log in, and which account each service runs as.
Who is here?

whoami            # current user
id                # uid, gid and group memberships
w                 # who is logged in right now
last -n 5         # the five most recent logins
cat /etc/passwd   # every account on the system
The three files behind it all

x: `/etc/passwd` — one line per account: `name:x:uid:gid:info:home:shell`. World-readable by design.
`/etc/shadow` — password hashes and expiry rules. Root-only, and that is the point.
`/etc/group` — group names plus members that are not the primary group.
uid `0` is root. Service accounts like `www-data` or `nobody` usually have `/usr/sbin/nologin` as their shell: they run services, humans cannot log in.

blocks.x: Create and manage a user

sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash ana   # home directory + bash shell
sudo passwd ana                    # set the password
sudo usermod -aG sudo ana          # add to sudo group (wheel on RHEL family)
groups ana                         # verify memberships
sudo userdel -r ana                # remove user and home directory
Always use `usermod -aG`. The `-a` means **append**: typing `-G` on its own replaces the entire group list and silently locks people out of things they could do yesterday.
Give every service its own unprivileged user. If the web app is compromised, the blast radius stops at what that one account can touch.

quiz.q: Where are password hashes stored?
quiz.why: `/etc/shadow` holds the hashes and is readable only by root. `/etc/passwd` contains account metadata but the password field just says `x`.

quiz.q: Add existing user ana to the sudo group on Ubuntu, without touching her other groups:
quiz.why: `-aG` appends. Plain `-G` replaces the whole group list — a classic way to break access by accident.

lessons.title: Root and sudo: power without bad habits
lessons.sum: Why you should not live as root, how sudo leaves receipts, and how to grant narrow powers instead of full control.

blocks.x: root (uid 0) can do anything: read every file, change every setting, kill every process. That is exactly why professionals do not live as root — they **escalate per command** with sudo.
Sudo: borrowed power, with receipts

sudo apt update            # run one command as root
sudo -i                    # start a root shell (know why, before you do)
sudo -u www-data whoami    # run as another user instead
sudo -l                    # what am I allowed to run?

x: Every sudo use is logged — usually in `/var/log/auth.log` (or `/var/log/secure` on RHEL family).
Sudo credentials are cached for a few minutes, so consecutive admin commands do not re-prompt.
`visudo` checks syntax **before** saving. Use it for every sudoers edit; a broken sudoers file can lock you out of admin rights entirely.

blocks.x: Grant narrow powers instead of full root

blocks.title: spot the difference
blocks.x:
sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/deploy

# full root — convenient, terrifying:
deploy ALL=(ALL) ALL

# narrow and auditable — restart ONE service, no password prompt:
deploy ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx
Automation (CI jobs, deploy scripts) needs `NOPASSWD` for a specific command — that is fine. Humans get a password prompt. Resist the urge to give both the same rule.
`sudo -i` out of habit is how wrong-window `rm -rf` stories happen: a root shell ignores every file permission safety net, and there is no trail of individual commands, just one root shell.

quiz.q: How should an administrator do daily work on a server?
opts: Always log in as root to save time
Log in as an unprivileged user and use sudo per command
Share the root password with the team
quiz.why: Least privilege with per-command escalation: every action is logged, and accidents stay small.

quiz.q: Where should you edit sudo rules?
quiz.why: `visudo` (and files in `/etc/sudoers.d/`) validates the syntax, so a typo cannot break sudo system-wide.

lessons.title: chmod, chown and the permission model
lessons.sum: Read any permission string at a glance, set exactly the access a file needs, and understand umask, owners and groups.

blocks.x: Linux permissions answer one question per file: **who can do what**. Get this model right once and you will debug 'permission denied' in seconds instead of reinstalling things.
Reading `ls -l`

-rwxr-xr--  1 deploy  www-data  4096 Oct  4 22:10 deploy.sh
│└┬┘└┬┘└┬┘    └owner  └group
│ │  │  └── others: r--
│ │  └───── group:  r-x
│ └──────── owner:  rwx
└────────── type: - file, d directory, l symlink

x: **r**ead = 4, **w**rite = 2, e**x**ecute = 1. Add them per role: `7` = rwx, `6` = rw-, `5` = r-x, `4` = r--.
Three digits = owner / group / others. `644` means owner reads and writes; everyone else only reads.

blocks.x: chmod in both styles

chmod 644 index.html         # rw-r--r--  typical file
chmod 755 deploy.sh          # rwxr-xr-x  scripts and directories
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519  # only I may read my private key
chmod +x backup.sh           # symbolic: add execute
chmod u+x,g-w notes.txt      # owner +execute, group -write
chown and chgrp: change who owns it

sudo chown deploy:www-data -R /srv/app
sudo chgrp www-data /srv/app/uploads
A typical web setup: files owned by the deploy user, group-owned by `www-data` (the account nginx or apache runs as), directories `755`, files `644`, secrets `600`, and your `.ssh` directory `700`.
umask: the defaults for new files

New files start from `666` minus the umask, new directories from `777` minus the umask. A umask of `022` produces the familiar 644/755 pair; a stricter `027` keeps the group from writing and others out entirely.

umask        # show the current mask
umask 027    # for this session — put it in ~/.profile to keep it
`chmod -R 777` is not a fix — it is a confession. World-writable files let any process rewrite your application. Find the right owner and group instead.

quiz.q: In symbolic form, `755` is:
quiz.why: 7 = rwx, 5 = r-x. So 755 expands to rwxr-xr-x: the owner can do everything, group and others can read and execute.

quiz.q: Set the owner of /srv/app to deploy and the group to www-data, recursively:
quiz.why: `chown owner:group path` changes both. `chmod` only changes permission bits, never ownership.

modules.title: Processes & Services
modules.sum: See what the machine is actually doing, stop and start things safely, and keep long-running services alive with systemd.

lessons.title: Processes, signals and load
lessons.sum: Inspect every running process, read load averages like a doctor reads an X-ray, and kill things without causing damage.

blocks.x: Every running thing on a server is a **process** with a numeric PID. When the machine feels slow or a service hangs, this is the layer you inspect first.
Look at what is running

ps aux                # every process, classic BSD style
ps aux | grep nginx   # the time-honoured filter
pgrep -a nginx        # PIDs plus command lines, by name
top                   # live view; q quits. htop is prettier
free -h               # memory and swap
uptime                # uptime and load averages

**Load average** (the three numbers from `uptime` or `top`) counts processes that want CPU or are stuck in I/O, averaged over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. Compare it to the core count (`nproc`): load 2.0 on a 2-core box means fully saturated; 8.0 on an 8-core box is business as usual.
Signals: ask nicely, then insist

kill 1234                  # SIGTERM (15): polite request to finish
kill -9 1234               # SIGKILL: kernel kills it — no cleanup
pkill -f 'node server.js'  # kill by command pattern
kill -HUP 1234             # SIGHUP (1): many daemons reload their config
Always try SIGTERM first. It lets the process flush data and close connections. SIGKILL skips all cleanup and can leave stale lock files, half-written files and corrupted state behind.
Foreground, background — and why services are different

./deploy.sh &        # start it in the background
jobs                 # what this shell has running
Ctrl+Z   then   bg   # suspend a foreground job, resume in background
nohup ./sync.sh &    # keep going even if SSH drops
disown               # fully detach from this shell
`nohup` and `&` are a stopgap: if the process crashes, nothing restarts it and nothing tells you. Anything that must keep running belongs in **systemd** — that is the next lesson.

quiz.q: Which signal asks a process to shut down gracefully?
quiz.why: SIGTERM lets the process save state and exit cleanly. Reserve SIGKILL for processes that ignore SIGTERM.

quiz.q: `uptime` reports a load average of 6.2 on a 2-core server. What does that mean?
opts: The machine is heavily oversubscribed — about 3× more work than it can run
quiz.why: Load roughly tracks runnable tasks; compare it with `nproc`. 6.2 on 2 cores means a long queue — usually I/O waits or CPU hogs.

lessons.title: systemd: services that survive reboots
lessons.sum: Start, stop, reload and enable services, then turn any long-running process into a proper systemd unit of your own.

blocks.x: Modern Linux boots with **systemd**: the init system starts as PID 1, then manages everything else as **units** — services, timers, mounts. One vocabulary for all of it.
Everyday systemctl

systemctl status nginx            # state + recent log lines
sudo systemctl start nginx        # start now
sudo systemctl stop nginx         # stop now
sudo systemctl restart nginx      # stop + start (connections drop)
sudo systemctl reload nginx       # re-read config, no downtime
sudo systemctl enable --now nginx # start now AND at every boot
systemctl is-enabled nginx        # will it come back after reboot?

`restart` kills the process tree and starts fresh; `reload` asks the service to re-read its config while staying up — users never notice. Use reload when supported, and `reload-or-restart` when you are not sure.
Poking around

systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running
systemctl list-units --failed     # what is broken right now?
systemctl cat nginx               # show the unit file(s) in use
systemctl list-timers             # scheduled jobs (cron's sibling)
Write your own service
Any long-running process can become a real service. One unit file buys you: survives reboots, restarts on crash, logs collected automatically in the journal.

blocks.title: /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service
blocks.x:
[Unit]
Description=My Node API
After=network.target

[Service]
User=app
WorkingDirectory=/srv/app
ExecStart=/usr/bin/node /srv/app/server.js
Restart=on-failure
Environment=NODE_ENV=production

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

sudo systemctl daemon-reload        # re-read unit files
sudo systemctl enable --now myapp   # start it and persist it
journalctl -u myapp -f              # watch its output live
Run `daemon-reload` after **every** unit file edit. Forgetting it is the number-one systemd confusion — systemd is still holding the old definition in memory.
Put your units in `/etc/systemd/system/`, never in `/usr/lib/systemd/system/` — package upgrades overwrite the latter. Local changes belong in `/etc`.

quiz.q: Which command makes nginx start automatically after a reboot?
quiz.why: `enable` links the unit into the boot targets; `start` only affects the current session. `enable --now` does both.

quiz.q: You edited `/etc/systemd/system/myapp.service`. What comes next?
quiz.why: systemd caches unit definitions. `daemon-reload` re-reads them, then restart (or reload) the service to apply.

lessons.title: Logs with journalctl and jobs with cron
lessons.sum: Read service logs like a detective, and schedule recurring jobs that actually run — and actually tell you when they fail.

blocks.x: Logs are how servers talk to you. systemd captures each service's output in the **journal**; classic text logs still live under `/var/log`. And for anything that must happen on schedule, cron has been the tool since forever.
journalctl: one service at a time

journalctl -u nginx -n 100        # last 100 lines for a unit
journalctl -u myapp -f            # follow live (Ctrl+C stops)
journalctl --since '1 hour ago'   # time window
journalctl -p err -b              # errors since the last boot
journalctl -u myapp --no-pager | tail -50
Classic log files

ls /var/log
sudo tail -f /var/log/auth.log        # logins + sudo (secure on RHEL)
sudo tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log
# watch which logs eat disk space:
du -sh /var/log/* | sort -h | tail -5
cron: schedule anything

crontab -e     # edit YOUR jobs  (sudo crontab -e for root's)
crontab -l     # list them

blocks.title: crontab anatomy
blocks.x:
# ┌─ minute (0-59)
# │ ┌─ hour (0-23)
# │ │ ┌─ day of month (1-31)
# │ │ │ ┌─ month (1-12)
# │ │ │ │ ┌─ weekday (0-7, Sunday is 0 or 7)
# │ │ │ │ │
  30 3 * * *  /usr/local/bin/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1

x: Shortcuts exist: `@daily`, `@hourly`, `@reboot`.
Job output is emailed — which in practice means **lost**. Always redirect: `>> /var/log/job.log 2>&1`.
Cron runs with a minimal environment. **Use absolute paths** in jobs, scripts and configs.
System-wide jobs can live in `/etc/cron.d/`, and modern replacements use systemd timers — check with `systemctl list-timers`.

blocks.x: Test every script by hand first, then in cron. The classic silent failure is a script that works in your shell because your interactive `PATH` was full of extras — cron's is almost empty.
A cron job that fails silently for a month is worse than no cron job. At minimum, log output with a timestamp; better still, make failures mail you or hit a heartbeat URL.

quiz.q: Show the last 100 log lines for the `myapp` service:
quiz.why: `-u` selects the unit and `-n 100` limits to the last 100 entries. Add `-f` to follow in real time.

quiz.q: Which crontab entry runs a backup every day at 03:30?
quiz.why: Fields run minute, hour, day, month, weekday. So `30 3 * * *` means minute 30 of hour 3, every day.

modules.title: Networking & Remote Access
modules.sum: Understand addresses, ports and DNS, log in with SSH keys, and move files around reliably.

lessons.title: Addresses, ports and DNS
lessons.sum: Check the four basics in the right order — address, route, listener, name — and debug 'it does not load' without guessing.

blocks.x: Servers exist to talk to other machines. When something 'is not working', disciplined people check four things in order instead of guessing. This lesson is the checklist.
1) Address and route

ip a                    # interfaces and IP addresses
ip r                    # routing table; 'default via' is the gateway
hostname -I             # just the IPs
ping -c 4 1.1.1.1       # is the network alive at all?
traceroute example.com  # hop by hop; find where it stalls
2) Listeners: is anything actually listening?

ss -tulpn               # TCP+UDP listeners with process names
ss -tulpn | grep ':443' # who owns port 443?
curl -I http://localhost:3000   # does the app answer on loopback?

x: Ports worth memorising: **22** SSH · **80** HTTP · **443** HTTPS · **5432** PostgreSQL · **3306** MySQL · **6379** Redis · **3000/8000** dev apps.
`127.0.0.1` is **loopback** — reachable only from this machine. `0.0.0.0` means every interface. An app bound to 127.0.0.1 is invisible to the outside no matter what the firewall says.

blocks.x: 3) DNS: is the name resolving?

dig +short example.com   # what IP does the name point to?
cat /etc/resolv.conf     # which resolvers are configured?
curl -sv https://example.com 2>&1 | head -25   # full request trace
The debugging order that saves hours

x: Is the process running? → `systemctl status myapp`
Is it listening? → `ss -tulpn | grep myport`
Does it answer locally? → `curl -I http://localhost:myport`
Is the firewall open? → `sudo ufw status`
Does the name resolve from outside? → `dig +short mydomain`

blocks.x: Each step eliminates a layer: process, socket, loopback, network stack, name. Fix the first step that fails and re-run the list — never skip downwards.

quiz.q: Which command shows listening ports along with the process that owns each one?
quiz.why: `ss -tulpn` lists TCP and UDP listeners (−t −u), listening only (−l), with process info (−p) and numeric ports (−n).

quiz.q: An app is bound to 127.0.0.1:8080. Can a client on the internet reach it?
opts: No — loopback is only reachable from the machine itself
quiz.why: Binding to the loopback interface means the socket never appears on the public interface. Bind to 0.0.0.0 (or the specific public IP) to accept outside connections.

lessons.title: SSH keys: log in like a professional
lessons.sum: Create a key pair, install the public half on servers, shortcut it with ~/.ssh/config, then harden the daemon safely.

blocks.x: SSH is your hands on the server. Passwords get guessed and brute-forced constantly; **keys** cannot be guessed at all. Set up key login first, then lock the door behind you.
Keys in sixty seconds

# on YOUR laptop:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C 'you@laptop'   # creates ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (+ .pub)
ssh-copy-id deploy@203.0.113.10         # installs the public key on the server
ssh deploy@203.0.113.10                 # now logs in without a password

x: `id_ed25519` is the **private key**: never leaves your laptop, never copied to a server, never committed to git. Keep it at `chmod 600`.
`id_ed25519.pub` is the **public key**: safe to share; it lands in `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` on each server you trust.
ed25519 is shorter and stronger than RSA. If you must use RSA: `-t rsa -b 4096`.

blocks.x: A config file that pays rent

blocks.title: ~/.ssh/config
blocks.x:
Host web
  HostName 203.0.113.10
  User deploy
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

# afterwards, just:   ssh web
Hardening the server: /etc/ssh/sshd_config

PasswordAuthentication no
PermitRootLogin no
AllowUsers deploy

# validate, then apply:
sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload sshd

**Never close your working session until key login succeeds in a second terminal.** Open a new window, run `ssh web`, and only then disable password auth. Locking yourself out of a remote server is a rite of passage you can skip.
Keep a passphrase on your key and let the agent remember it for the session: `eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"` then `ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519`. Key-grade security, password-grade convenience.

quiz.q: Which piece ends up on the server for key-based login?
quiz.why: The server stores public keys; your laptop proves ownership of the matching private key during login. The private key never travels.

quiz.q: Safe order for disabling password logins?
opts: Set PasswordAuthentication no first, then test
Test key login in a second session, then set PasswordAuthentication no and reload sshd
Disable SSH and use the console
quiz.why: Prove the new path works while the old one is still open — then close the old one. One terminal too few is how people lock themselves out.

lessons.title: Moving files: scp, rsync, sftp
lessons.sum: Ship code, pull logs and sync trees between machines — with dry runs before anything destructive.

blocks.x: You will move files between machines constantly: deploy code, pull logs, ship a database dump. Each tool has a sweet spot — know which one to reach for.
Pick the right tool

x: **scp** — one file or one small directory, right now. Dead simple, no resume.
**rsync** — everything bigger: whole trees, only transfers changes, resumable, can mirror deletions.
**sftp** — interactive browsing and transfers when you want to walk the tree first.

blocks.x:
scp report.pdf deploy@web:/srv/reports/       # one file up
scp deploy@web:/var/log/nginx/access.log ./   # one file down
scp -r site/ deploy@web:/var/www/              # small directory

rsync -avz --progress site/ deploy@web:/var/www/  # fast sync of a tree
rsync -avn site/ deploy@web:/var/www/             # dry run: what WOULD change?
rsync -avz --delete site/ deploy@web:/var/www/    # mirror, deleting extras
rsync -avz deploy@web:/var/log/ ./logs/           # pull logs down
The **trailing slash matters**: `site/` copies the *contents* of site; `site` without the slash copies the directory itself into the destination.
Sanity rules

x: Dry-run (`-n`) whenever `--delete` is on the table — see the plan before it executes.
`-P` gives per-file progress and lets interrupted transfers resume.
Exclude the noise on code deploys: `--exclude '.git' --exclude 'node_modules'`.
On slow or flaky links, rsync beats scp every time: it continues where it stopped.

blocks.x: `rsync -a` preserves permissions, timestamps and symlinks. Add hardlinks, ACLs and attributes (`-aHAX`) when you are building serious backups.
`rsync --delete` makes the destination **exactly** match the source — deletions included. One typo in the source path can therefore wipe the destination. Dry-run it. Then dry-run it again.

quiz.q: Which tool resumes interrupted transfers and only sends changed parts?
quiz.why: rsync compares both ends and transfers only the differences — ideal for large trees and unstable connections.

quiz.q: What is the difference between `rsync -a site/ dest/` and `rsync -a site dest/`?
opts: The trailing slash copies the contents of site; without it, the whole site directory is placed inside dest
The trailing slash makes it recursive
Without the slash it only copies files, not subdirectories
quiz.why: With `site/`, dest receives site's contents directly. Without it, you get dest/site/… — the classic rsync gotcha.

modules.title: Server Setup & Security
modules.sum: Install and update software the right way, serve a real website with nginx and TLS, then lock the machine down and back it up.

lessons.title: Packages: install, update, inspect
lessons.sum: Use the package manager for everything, read the Debian vs Red Hat differences, and let security updates install themselves.

blocks.x: Every piece of software on the server — nginx, PostgreSQL, even your shell — came from a **package manager** pulling signed packages from repositories. It is how you install, update and remove software without chasing downloads.
The everyday commands (Debian/Ubuntu: apt)

sudo apt update              # refresh the package lists (no upgrades yet)
sudo apt upgrade -y          # install available upgrades
sudo apt install nginx       # install; dependencies come along automatically
sudo apt remove nginx        # uninstall (purge also removes its configs)
apt list --upgradable        # what is waiting to be updated?
`update` refreshes the catalog; `upgrade` installs from it. They are two different jobs — forgetting `update` first is why people 'cannot find' a package that clearly exists.
Red Hat family: dnf

sudo dnf upgrade --refresh   # update everything
sudo dnf install nginx
sudo dnf remove nginx
dnf info nginx               # description + version
Search and inspect

apt search 'web server'    # search names and descriptions
apt show nginx             # version, size, dependencies, homepage
dpkg -l | grep nginx       # what version is actually installed?
nginx -v                   # ask the software itself
Let security updates install themselves

sudo apt install unattended-upgrades
sudo dpkg-reconfigure --priority=low unattended-upgrades

# later, check what it did:
cat /var/log/unattended-upgrades/unattended-upgrades.log
Only add third-party repositories (PPAs, custom apt sources) that you genuinely trust. A repository is software installation with root rights — treat adding one like handing someone your SSH key.

quiz.q: What does `sudo apt update` actually do?
opts: Refreshes the list of available packages and versions
Upgrades the distribution to the next release
quiz.why: `update` syncs the catalog from repositories. `upgrade` (or `full-upgrade`) installs newer versions — usually the next thing you run.

quiz.q: Which command shows the version of nginx that is installed right now?
quiz.why: `dpkg -l` lists installed packages and their versions. `apt show` describes what the repository offers, not what is on disk.

lessons.title: Serving a real site with nginx
lessons.sum: Install nginx, serve a static site, reverse-proxy an app on port 3000, and add free TLS with certbot.

blocks.x: Time to serve something real. nginx is the workhorse of the modern web: static file server, reverse proxy and TLS terminator in one small binary.
Install and check

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y nginx
sudo systemctl enable --now nginx
curl -I http://localhost
# → HTTP/1.1 200 OK   ·   Server: nginx
Serve a static site
On Debian/Ubuntu, sites live in `/etc/nginx/sites-available/` and are switched on by symlinking into `sites-enabled/` — exactly the symlink pattern you already know.

blocks.title: /etc/nginx/sites-available/mysite

blocks.x:
sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/mysite /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/
sudo mkdir -p /var/www/mysite
echo 'hello from nginx' | sudo tee /var/www/mysite/index.html
sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx   # test FIRST, then reload
Reverse proxy: put nginx in front of your app
Apps usually listen on a high port on loopback (say 3000). nginx accepts public traffic on 80/443 and forwards it — adding TLS, compression and caching, and giving you one place to manage domains.
TLS in three commands

sudo apt install certbot python3-certbot-nginx
sudo certbot --nginx -d example.com -d www.example.com
# certbot edits the vhost, fetches the certificate, sets up auto-renewal
systemctl list-timers | grep certbot   # the renewal timer
`nginx -t` before every reload, and `journalctl -u nginx -n 50` when it misbehaves. A wrong `proxy_pass` port is the most common culprit by far.
Keep the site root owned by your deploy user but **readable** by the nginx user (`www-data`). The web server must be able to read files — never to write them.

quiz.q: Which command validates nginx configuration before you reload?
quiz.why: `nginx -t` parses the config and reports syntax errors — a reload with a broken config takes the site down.

quiz.q: What does a reverse proxy do?
opts: Accepts client traffic and forwards it to your app, adding TLS and control
Replaces the need for a firewall
quiz.why: nginx terminates the public connection and proxies to the app on loopback — the app stays hidden, and TLS/compression/routing live in one place.

quiz.q: On Ubuntu, where do site configurations live before being enabled?
quiz.why: Sites live in `sites-available/` and are activated with a symlink into `sites-enabled/` — easy to disable without deleting.

lessons.title: Firewalls: close everything, open what you need
lessons.sum: Default-deny with ufw or firewalld, keep SSH open, and remember the second firewall waiting in the cloud dashboard.

blocks.x: A firewall is the list of doors that exist on your server. The professional default: **close everything**, then open exactly what is needed — starting with SSH, or you will lock yourself out of your own machine.
ufw: the friendly firewall (Ubuntu/Debian)

sudo ufw allow OpenSSH     # FIRST: keep your own door open
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp
sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw status verbose     # what is open, and the default policy
sudo ufw delete allow 80/tcp                        # remove a rule
sudo ufw allow from 203.0.113.7 to any port 5432    # DB for one host only
firewalld: the Red Hat family equivalent

sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=https
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all
How to think about a firewall

x: Open by **service** (`OpenSSH`, `http`) or by **port** (`443/tcp`). Both styles are fine.
Anything not explicitly allowed is dropped. That is the whole point.
Databases should almost never answer from the entire internet. Allow the one host that needs access, not `0.0.0.0/0`.
Compare two lists regularly: what is listening (`ss -tulpn`) versus what is open (`ufw status`). They should match closely.

blocks.x: Enabling a firewall over SSH with the wrong rules is how people lose access to servers. Allow SSH **first**, then enable — and keep your provider's console open in another tab the first time.
Cloud servers usually have a **second firewall**: the security group in the provider's dashboard. A port open in `ufw` but closed in the security group is still unreachable. Check both layers.

quiz.q: Which rule must exist before you run `sudo ufw enable` on a remote server?
quiz.why: Without an SSH rule, enabling the default-deny firewall cuts the connection you are using to enable it.

quiz.q: A port is open in ufw but unreachable from the internet. Most likely reason?
opts: The cloud provider's security group (the second firewall) does not allow it
quiz.why: Cloud VMs typically filter traffic twice: once in the provider network layer and once on the host. Both must allow the port.

lessons.title: Hardening habits and backups worth the name
lessons.sum: Five habits that keep a server safe over years, fail2ban against brute-forcers, and backups with the 3-2-1 rule.

blocks.x: A fresh server is a stranger; a managed server is a home. Five habits turn one into the other — and the last one matters because the first four can still fail.
The five habits

x: **Patch automatically.** Unattended upgrades plus reboots when the kernel changes. Most breaches are known bugs fixed months earlier.
**Minimise exposure.** Nothing listens that does not have to (`ss -tulpn`), the firewall is default-deny, SSH is key-only.
**Least privilege.** Services run as their own users, humans escalate with sudo, nothing runs as root that does not need to.
**Watch.** Check failed logins (`/var/log/auth.log`), let fail2ban punish repeat offenders, and keep one outside uptime check.
**Back up.** Assume disk failure, fat fingers and ransomware. And assume your restore will be tested — an untested backup is a rumour.

blocks.x: fail2ban: automatic banning

sudo apt install fail2ban
sudo cp /etc/fail2ban/jail.conf /etc/fail2ban/jail.local   # local overrides

# in jail.local:
[sshd]
enabled = true
maxretry = 5
bantime = 1h

sudo systemctl enable --now fail2ban
sudo fail2ban-client status sshd    # see bans and current blocks
Backups worth the name: 3-2-1

x: **3** copies of the data, **2** different media, **1** off-site. A backup on the same disk is just a copy of the accident.
Automated via cron or a systemd timer — discipline is not a backup strategy.
Versioned: never overwrite yesterday. A corrupted file syncs its corruption to every destination instantly.
Restores are tested. Untested backups are decoration.

blocks.title: Space-efficient snapshots
blocks.x:
rsync -a --delete --link-dest=/backups/latest /srv/app/ /backups/2026-10-04/
# unchanged files become hardlinks → a full-looking snapshot at near-zero cost
ls -l /backups/    # each dated folder looks complete; the disk only stores changes

For the off-site copy, prefer a **pull**: the backup host connects out and fetches. The production server then holds no credentials to your backup infrastructure — the most valuable target stays out of reach.
Never call something a backup system until you have restored from it at least once — one file, then one directory, onto a scratch machine. Do it before the day you really need it, not during.

quiz.q: What does the 3-2-1 rule mean?
opts: 3 copies of data, on 2 kinds of media, with 1 off-site
3 backups per day, 2 per week, 1 per month
quiz.why: Three copies guard against corruption, two media types against a bad disk batch, and one off-site copy against fire, theft and ransomware.

quiz.q: You have automated backups but never restored anything. Which statement is true?
opts: The backups are unverified — restore one before trusting them
Restores are unnecessary if the job exits 0
You should back up twice as often
quiz.why: An exit code of 0 only proves the script ran. Only a restore proves the data is there and readable.

modules.title: Shell Scripting
modules.sum: Turn your command line knowledge into reusable scripts with variables, control flow and honest error handling.

lessons.title: Your first bash script
lessons.sum: Shebangs, variables, quoting and exit codes — the anatomy every good script shares.

blocks.x: The moment you type the same three commands twice, a script starts paying for itself. Bash is already installed on every server — no runtime to deploy, no excuses.
A small, complete example

blocks.title: backup-notes.sh
blocks.x:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail        # stop on errors, unset vars, failing pipes

NAME="demo"
TARGET="/srv/app"
TODAY=$(date +%F)

echo "Backing up $TARGET"
tar -czf "/tmp/$NAME-$TODAY.tar.gz" "$TARGET"
echo "Done: /tmp/$NAME-$TODAY.tar.gz"
Make it runnable

chmod +x backup-notes.sh   # sets the execute bit
./backup-notes.sh          # run it
bash backup-notes.sh       # or run without the bit
bash -x backup-notes.sh    # trace each command as it runs (debugging)
Variables and quoting

NAME='web-01'          # no spaces around the equals sign!
echo "Hello $NAME"     # double quotes: variable expands
echo 'Hello $NAME'     # single quotes: literal text
echo "${NAME}_bak"     # braces mark where the name ends

echo "script: $0 · first arg: $1 · all args: $@ · count: $#"
readonly LOG_DIR=/var/log
The safety header: set -euo pipefail

x: `set -e` — exit immediately when a command fails.
`set -u` — treat undefined variables as errors (typos stop the script instead of silently doing nothing).
`set -o pipefail` — a pipeline fails if **any** stage fails, not just the last one.
Exit codes: `0` = success, non-zero = failure. Cron, CI and other scripts read these — end honestly.

blocks.x: Prefer `#!/usr/bin/env bash` over `#!/bin/bash`: the script then uses whichever bash is first on the PATH, which keeps it portable to BSD and macOS machines.
Never `eval` input you did not construct, and always quote variables: `rm -rf "$DIR"/` with an empty `DIR` is the classic disaster. `set -u` exists precisely for this.

quiz.q: What does the `set -euo pipefail` line protect you from?
opts: Continuing after failures, undefined variables, and hidden pipeline errors
quiz.why: It is the three-part seatbelt of bash: fail fast, catch typos, and don't let a pipeline hide a failing stage.

quiz.q: How does a script signal failure to whatever called it?
opts: Printing an error to the screen
quiz.why: The exit code is the contract. `exit 1` (or any non-zero) makes `&&` chains, cron and CI treat the run as failed.

lessons.title: Conditions, loops and functions
lessons.sum: Make scripts think: if/else, case, loops, functions and the trap that cleans up after you.

blocks.x: Scripts become programs when they can make decisions and repeat work. That is all control flow is: conditions, loops, and a little tidying up afterwards.
Conditions

if [ ! -d "$TARGET" ]; then
  echo "missing: $TARGET" >&2
  exit 1
fi

if grep -q 'ERROR' "$LOG"; then
  echo 'errors found in the log'
else
  echo 'all clean'
fi

x: File tests: `-f` exists and is a file · `-d` directory · `-z` string empty · `-n` string not empty.
Comparisons: `[ "$a" = "$b" ]` strings · `[ "$n" -gt 5 ]` numbers (`-gt -lt -ge -le -eq -ne`).
Combine tests with separate brackets: `[ -f "$f" ] && [ -r "$f" ]` — not `-a` inside one bracket.

blocks.x: Loops

for site in /var/www/*; do
  echo "site: $site ($(du -sh "$site" | cut -f1))"
done

while read -r host; do
  echo "checking $host"
done < server-list.txt

for i in 1 2 3; do echo "attempt $i"; done
case: multi-way decisions
Functions and traps
`trap cleanup EXIT` is the mark of a careful script: temp files, lock files and partial downloads get removed no matter how the script ends — including when it crashes.
Never loop over a file with `for line in $(cat file)` — it splits on spaces, not lines. Use `while read -r line; do ... done < file` instead.

quiz.q: Which test is true only when `$PATHVAR` points to an existing directory?
quiz.why: `-d` tests for a directory; `-f` is for regular files; `-z` checks for an empty string.

quiz.q: How do you safely iterate over the lines of a file?
quiz.why: `while read -r` preserves lines with spaces and special characters. `for ... $(cat file)` word-splits and mangles them.

lessons.title: Project: a backup script you can keep
lessons.sum: Combine everything into a real script: error handling, logging, rotation, cron scheduling — and the discipline to test it.

blocks.x: Time to combine everything you have learned into one artifact: a backup script with logging, rotation and honest error handling. Copy it, change two paths, and it is yours.

blocks.title: /usr/local/bin/backup-app.sh
blocks.x:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

SRC="/srv/app"
DEST="/backups/app"
KEEP=7
STAMP=$(date +%F_%H%M)
LOG="/var/log/backup-app.log"

log() { echo "[$(date '+%F %T')] $*" | tee -a "$LOG"; }

if [ ! -d "$SRC" ]; then
  log "ERROR: source $SRC is missing"
  exit 1
fi

mkdir -p "$DEST/$STAMP"
log "start: $SRC -> $DEST/$STAMP"

rsync -a --delete "$SRC/" "$DEST/$STAMP/"

# rotation: keep the newest $KEEP snapshots, remove the rest
ls -1dt "$DEST"/*/ | tail -n +$((KEEP + 1)) | xargs -r rm -rf

log "done: $(du -sh "$DEST/$STAMP" | cut -f1) archived"
What each piece buys you

x: `set -euo pipefail` plus the source check: it fails loudly instead of quietly producing a series of empty backups.
`log()` with `tee -a`: every line goes to stdout **and** to the log file — cron output and a paper trail in one.
A timestamped destination directory: each run is a new snapshot; nothing overwrites yesterday.
Rotation: `ls -1dt` sorts by time, `tail -n +8` skips the newest seven, `xargs -r rm -rf` deletes the rest. The `-r` means do nothing on an empty list — it has prevented many disasters.

blocks.x: Install it properly

sudo install -m 755 backup-app.sh /usr/local/bin/backup-app.sh
sudo /usr/local/bin/backup-app.sh     # run once by hand — always

sudo crontab -e
# add:
0 3 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup-app.sh >> /var/log/backup-app.log 2>&1

tail -f /var/log/backup-app.log       # watch the next run land
Level it up later

x: Switch to `--link-dest` snapshots (previous module) when disk space matters.
Push one copy off-site daily — pull, not push, when you can.
Add a heartbeat: alert when the last successful run is older than 26 hours.
Run a restore drill on a scratch machine. Only then may you call it a backup system.

blocks.x: Put this script in version control. The backup script is the one script on your server that must still work two years from now — treat it with the respect you would give production code.
Test with a **scratch destination** the first time. A `--delete` pointed at the wrong path does not warn you; it simply makes the mistake perfectly synchronised.

quiz.q: Why run the script by hand before installing the cron entry?
opts: Because cron failures are silent — a manual run proves paths, permissions and output work
Cron cannot run scripts that were never run manually
To warm up the disk cache
quiz.why: Cron jobs fail quietly by default. A manual run under the same user and environment catches the problems while you are watching.

quiz.q: Which line stops the snapshots from filling the disk?
opts: The rotation line that keeps only the newest `$KEEP` folders
quiz.why: Without rotation every snapshot is kept forever. The `ls -1dt | tail | xargs rm` line keeps the newest seven and discards the rest.
